questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I already lived there once and had a grab on the German language, which I wanted to make even better - both for personal reasons and because German is a crucial language inside the world of theology (which I study). Berlin (where I was) - and Germany in general - is an epicenter of theology, and I wanted to experience that from the inside. 
Also, I wanted to go to Berlin to experience its history, its multiculturalism, its art scene, its colors, all of the things that attracts most people to the city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was all right. I was helped much by the contact person at the faculty at HU.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received some assistance from the administration office, but because we were only three exchange students at the faculty, we had to figure out many things ourselves that were not natural for us to know. For instance when it came to collecting ECTS-point and what subjects we where supposed to choose. Never the less, there were administrative people there expecting our arrival and telling us what to do, and that was nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Not easy. There was and still is many problems with the people I have been renting the apartment from. Looking back, I wish I had stayed at a dormitory.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There is a chance that you will meet people outside of the study world. I did, and that was really great. However, it is much more of a lonely - and, for me: frustrating - process because there is no institution to set the rules and no students or like-minded to include you in their community.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to fulfill different requirements respectively from the administrative office at Copenhagen University and the administrative office at Humboldt-Universität. It was clear that they had two different systems with two different ambitions for the students.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was actually quite flexible to register at Humboldt: the teachers and the administrative people were openminded and helpfull. However, during the stay, it turned out that one of the classes, I was following and Copenhagen had accepted, wouldn't be able to live up to their own requirements for ECTS-points. Very unfortunate. I also had doubts all way about which person in Copenhagen, I should contact with my questions. That was not the case at Humboldt.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was able to register at the classes I wanted at Humboldt. However, as mentioned above, it wasn't all of the classes that turned out to be acceptable for Copenhagen - and that made me very uncertain in the process.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure that the two institutions are not - figuratively - speaking two different languages. Talk to a person who have been abroad were you are going, since that is often the expert - not the administration offices.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was very good. The teachers were very attentive, and all of the courses felt relevant and important. There was a good conversation between teacher and students, meaningful discussions, where the student's words and opinions were taken at face value.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: More students were involved at HU than at CPH. It was less formal at HU than at CPH, more natural to debate with the teachers. Spaces were created that were more about learning and being curios than about how to get through an exam. Generally very little - if any - focus on exams in the classrooms.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- “Das Böse denken” - eine praktisch-theologische Auseinandersetzung mit Hannah Arendt bei Lina Hildebrandt-Wackwitz (UE)

- Hannah Arendt: deutsch jüdisches Denkens bei Amir Engel (SE) 

- Säkulares Judentum: eine Untersuchung bei Amir Engel (VL) 

- König David bei Meik Gerhards (SE)

- Zorn und Gewalt Gottes nach dem Buch Zefanja bei Markus Witte (SE)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Especially the courses with Amir Engel. They were vibrant and relevant and were not dictated by form and formalities.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
- I had to rent a bike, because my own broke
- I lost almost all of my deposit to the apartment I was renting due to an unaccountable landlord
- In general: public transportation - trains and busses that didn't arrive at time, meaning I had to pay double or triple for tickets

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transportation was more expensive. The costs for living in an apartment and not being treated fairly by the landlord was more expensive. 

Foods, drinks, concerts and so on were less expensive than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I went to sports every monday through Humboldt. Otherwise, I didn't experience that many social or cultural activities were available.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to concerts, to the museum, in cinemas, go drink beers ind different areas, go to a sport and meet people there.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See the city where you live. Bike around. Go to flea markets.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was alright. In general, people were very friendly and open minded.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Maybe the fact that I had to say 'Herr' and 'Frau' and 'Sie' instead of 'du'. That was a challenge, because I'm not used to that.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The open-mindedness. The patience and the goodwill when it came to my German.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Make sure that you want to learn and speak German throughout. There is almost no English during the stay. 
2) Find a dormitory or another institutional place instead of renting an apartment privately. 
3) Try to establish contact to a person from your home university who already went to the place were you are going abroad - that person can be a good life guard, who most likely already experienced, what you are going through.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to register at a language school before the semester starts! That is a very convenient way to start to speak German and to land in the city.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: That I am now able to speak German.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Administrative and bureaucratic stuff.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
